UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Ivan D. Davis

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO DISQUALIFY
MAGISTRATE JUDGE IVAN D. DAVIS UNDER 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) AND § 455(a),
AND FOR PRIORITY DETERMINATION

I. INTRODUCTION

Magistrate Judge Davis’s two most recent annual financial disclosure reports list “FB
common stock.” Ex. A at 2 (Part VII, line 6); Ex. B at 4 (Part VII, line 6). Each report assigns the
holding a year-end value of $15,001 to $50,000. Judge Davis signed the 2025 report on May 14,
2026 and May 26, 2026. Ex. A at 1. “FB” was the trading symbol of Facebook, Inc. Facebook, Inc.
is Meta Platforms, Inc. Meta is a defendant in this action.

Plaintiff filed this action on July 30, 2026. Judge Davis has since entered six orders. The
last of them, ECF No. 84, denied discovery directed to Meta and denied leave to amend. Section

455(b)(4) requires a magistrate judge who knows that he has a financial interest in a party to

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 15 PagelD# 851

disqualify himself. Section 455(d)(4) defines a financial interest as ownership of a legal or
equitable interest “however small.” Section 455(e) bars the parties from waiving that ground.

The reports establish the holding at the end of 2024 and at the end of 2025. They do not
establish the holding in August, September, or October 2026. The present record cannot resolve
that fact. The Court can. This Motion asks that the fact be stated on the record and that the statute be
applied to it.

II. STATEMENT OF FACTS

A. The disclosure reports. Exhibit A is the Financial Disclosure Report (AO Form
10) of “Davis, Ivan,” Magistrate Judge, U.S. District Court, Virginia Eastern, for calendar year
2025. It bears two electronic signatures: May 14, 2026 at 1:34 p.m. and May 26, 2026 at 9:57 a.m.
Ex. A at 1. Each signature follows this certification: “I certify that all information given above
(including information pertaining to my spouse and minor or dependent children, if any) is
accurate, true, and complete to the best of my knowledge and belief.” Id. Part VII, line 6, reads:
“FB common stock,” income “$1,000 or less,” income type “Dividend,” gross value “$15,001 -
$50,000,” value method “Cash/Market.” Ex. A at 2. Line 6 reports no transaction. Lines 37 through
40 report sales and purchases of four other securities on August 21, 2025. Ex. A at 3.

Exhibit B is the Financial Disclosure Report of “Davis, Ivan D.,” U.S. Magistrate Judge,
full-time, for the reporting period January 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024, dated August 18, 2025.
Ex. B at 1. Part VII, line 6, reads: “FB common stock,” income code A, income type “Dividend,”
value code K, value method T. Ex. B at 4. The report’s legend defines code A as “$1,000 or less,”
code K as “$15,001 - $50,000,” and code T as “Cash Market.” Id. Line 6 reports no transaction. The
report’s certification, signed “s/ Ivan D. Davis,” uses the same “accurate, true, and complete to the

best of my knowledge and belief” language. Ex. B at 8.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 15 PagelD# 852

Both reports identify common-stock holdings by trading symbol. Ex. A at 2—3 (lines 4-6,
16-34); Ex. B at 4-6 (lines 4-6, 16-18, 20-35). Both reports list mutual funds and exchange-traded
funds as separate line items. Ex. A at 2—3 (lines 2, 3, 11, 12, 18, 35); Ex. B at 4—6 (lines 2, 3, 11, 12,
18, 36). Both reports list an IRA as a separate line item. Ex. A at 3 (line 36); Ex. B at 6 (line 37).

B. Facebook, Inc. is Meta Platforms, Inc. The Class A common stock of Facebook,
Inc. traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the symbol “FB.” Meta Platforms, Inc., Annual
Report (Form 10-K) for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2021 (filed Feb. 3, 2022) (cover page). On
October 28, 2021, Facebook, Inc. amended its certificate of incorporation to change its name to
Meta Platforms, Inc. Facebook, Inc., Current Report (Form 8-K) (Oct. 28, 2021); Meta Platforms,
Inc., Annual Report (Form 10-K) for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2021 (filed Feb. 3, 2022). In
June 2022, the trading symbol for the same Class A common stock changed from “FB” to
“META.” Meta Platforms, Inc., Annual Report (Form 10-K) for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31,
2022 (filed Feb. 2, 2023) (cover page). Federal courts treat the two names as one company. Mirror
Worlds Techs., LLC v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 122 F.4th 860 (Fed. Cir. 2024) (identifying Meta
Platforms, Inc. as the company formerly known as Facebook, Inc.).

The reports for 2024 and 2025 continue to describe the asset as “FB common stock.” The
description supports an inference that line 6 denotes common stock of Meta Platforms, Inc.
Plaintiff asks the Court to confirm that inference. Mot. Part V(a).

C. Meta’s party status and Judge Davis’s participation. Meta has been a named
defendant since July 30, 2026. ECF Nos. 1, 5. Meta moved to dismiss and filed its corporate
disclosure statement on August 21, 2026. ECF Nos. 21, 22, 24. Magistrate Judge Davis is the
assigned magistrate judge. Hearings on Plaintiff’s motions were set before him on August 25 and

September 8, 2026. He entered ECF Nos. 62, 63, and 64 on September 9, 2026; ECF No. 65 on

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 4 of 15 PagelD# 853

September 10, 2026; ECF No. 82 on September 22, 2026; and ECF No. 84 on October 7, 2026.
ECF No. 84 denied ECF Nos. 15 and 54 as premature, describing them as requests for expedited
discovery concerning NCMEC and “Meta Platforms, Inc., respectively,” and denied ECF No. 59
for noncompliance with ECF No. 64. ECF No. 84 at 1-2. The docket reflects no disclosure of the
reported holding to the parties.

D. Discovery and submission. Plaintiff was unaware of the reported financial interest
when ECF No. 84 was entered and promptly presented this Motion after learning of it. Ballentine
Decl. { 2. Plaintiff retrieved Exhibits A and B from the Financial Disclosure Reports database
maintained by the Administrative Office of the United States Courts. Id. 44] 3—4.

E. Related proceedings. ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76 are pending before District Judge
Alston. On October 12, 2026, Plaintiff submitted through the Court’s Electronic Document
Submission System a Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument as to ECF Nos. 66, 67, and 76,
requesting determination of those motions on the papers under Local Civil Rule 7(J). Concurrently
with this Motion, Plaintiff submits Rule 72(a) objections to ECF No. 84 and an application to
District Judge Alston concerning the referral and retrospective relief. This Memorandum does not
repeat the arguments in those filings.

Til. ARGUMENT

A. Direct Ownership of Common Stock in a Party Requires Disqualification
Under § 455(b)(4).
1. The statutory elements. Section 455 applies to “[a]ny justice, judge, or magistrate

judge of the United States.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(a). Section 455(b)(4) requires disqualification where
the judge “knows that he, individually or as a fiduciary, or his spouse or minor child residing in his
household, has a financial interest in the subject matter in controversy or in a party to the

proceeding.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4). The elements are a covered officer, a financial interest,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 5 of 15 PagelD# 854

knowledge, and a party. Judge Davis is a covered officer. Meta is a party. ECF Nos. 1, 5, 21, 24.
The remaining elements are the financial interest and knowledge.

2. Common stock is a financial interest regardless of amount. Section 455(d)(4)
defines “financial interest” as “ownership of a legal or equitable interest, however small.” The
Fourth Circuit reads those words as written. “If a judge has an ownership interest in a party or in the
subject matter in controversy, it matters not at all whether the interest is a large or infinitesimally
small amount.” In re Va. Elec. & Power Co., 539 F.2d 357, 368 (4th Cir. 1976). “[I]t is well-
established that the ownership of stock constitutes a ‘financial interest’” under § 455(b)(4). Cent.
Tel. Co. of Va. v. Sprint Commc’ns Co. of Va., Inc., 715 F.3d 501, 515 (4th Cir. 2013) (quoting
Shell Oil Co. v. United States, 672 F.3d 1283, 1289 (Fed. Cir. 2012)). The Fourth Circuit “read[s] §
455(b)(4) to require a judge who is a stockholder in a party to a case to disqualify himself from
participation in the case even when he is not the fact-finder.” Gladhill v. Gen. Motors Corp., 743
F.2d 1049, 1051 (4th Cir. 1984). Gladhill concerned a juror who owned stock in a party. The court
cited § 455(b)(4) as the legislative rule confirming that a stockholder in a party may not sit. Id. The
reported holding here is common stock. The statute makes its amount irrelevant.

3. The fund exception does not appear on the face of the reports. Section 455(d)(4)
(i) provides that “[o]wnership in a mutual or common investment fund that holds securities is not a
‘financial interest’ in such securities unless the judge participates in the management of the fund.”
In Central Telephone, the judge held the shares in an IRA “along with the assets of many others
who hold similar accounts,” and the fund managers made the buy and sell decisions “without input
from the presiding judge.” 715 F.3d at 516. The Fourth Circuit held that the exception applied and
that no financial interest existed. Id. The reports here describe line 6 as “common stock.” They list

the judge’s funds separately. They list the judge’s IRA separately. Ex. A at 2-3; Ex. B at 4-6. On its

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 6 of 15 PagelD# 855

face, line 6 is a direct holding. Whether the stock is held through an arrangement that qualifies
under § 455(d)(4)(i) is a fact within Judge Davis’s knowledge. The Motion asks that it be stated.
Mot. Part V(d).

A, Knowledge. Section 455(b)(4) applies when the judge “knows” of the interest.
Liljeberg v. Health Servs. Acquisition Corp., 486 U.S. 847, 859 (1988). Section 455(c) directs a
judge to “inform himself about his personal and fiduciary financial interests.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(c).
Two facts bear on knowledge. The first is knowledge of the holding. Judge Davis certified on May
14 and May 26, 2026 that the 2025 report was “accurate, true, and complete to the best of my
knowledge and belief.” Ex. A at 1. He certified the 2024 report in the same terms on August 18,
2025. Ex. B at 8. Those certifications support an inference that Judge Davis knew, as of May 26,
2026, that he had reported holding FB common stock at the close of 2025. The second is
knowledge that the issuer is a party. Meta’s name appears in the caption of every filing. ECF No. 84
names “Meta Platforms, Inc.” and rules on discovery directed to Meta. ECF No. 84 at 1. The docket
establishes Meta’s participation. Whether Judge Davis connected the reported holding with the
party is a fact the Motion asks the Court to state. In Central Telephone, the appellant relied on the
judge’s financial disclosure form to establish knowledge. 715 F.3d at 515. The Fourth Circuit did
not reach that question because the fund exception applied. Id. at 516. No fund exception appears
here.

5. Nonwaiver. Section 455(e) bars a judge from accepting from the parties a waiver of
any ground enumerated in subsection (b). “Under § 455(e), the judge may not even accept a waiver
of this disqualification from the parties.” Gladhill, 743 F.2d at 1051; see also Centripetal
Networks, Inc. v. Cisco Sys., Inc., 38 F.4th 1025 (Fed. Cir. 2022) (“Recusal under § 455(a) may be

waived, but recusal under § 455(b) cannot be waived.”). Plaintiff offers no waiver. No party can.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 7 of 15 PagelD# 856

B. Section 455(a) Independently Requires Consideration of Disqualification.

Section 455(a) requires disqualification in any proceeding in which the judge’s
“impartiality might reasonably be questioned.” The test is objective. “The critical question
presented by this statute ‘is not whether the judge is impartial in fact. It is simply whether another,
not knowing whether or not the judge is actually impartial, might reasonably question his
impartiality on the basis of all the circumstances.’” United States v. DeTemple, 162 F.3d 279, 286
(4th Cir. 1998) (quoting Hathcock v. Navistar Int’! Transp. Corp., 53 F.3d 36, 41 (4th Cir. 1995)).
The observer is “a person outside the judicial system,” and “not a person unduly suspicious or
concemed about a trivial risk that a judge may be biased.” Id. at 287. Section 455(a) requires no
knowledge. Congress “intended to require knowledge under subsection (b)(4) and not to require
knowledge under subsection (a).” Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 859. The provision’s purpose “does not
depend upon whether or not the judge actually knew of facts creating an appearance of impropriety,
so long as the public might reasonably believe that he or she knew.” Id. at 860.

Facts that fall short under § 455(b) remain relevant under § 455(a). “Even where the facts
do not suffice for recusal under § 455(b), however, those same facts may be examined as part of an
inquiry into whether recusal is mandated under § 455(a).” In re Certain Underwriter Defs., 294
F.3d 297, 306 (2d Cir. 2002). The Second Circuit applied that rule to a district judge whose spouse
held stock in a defendant during part of the case. Litovich v. Bank of Am. Corp., 106 F.4th 218 (2d
Cir. 2024) (per curiam). The record there did not show when the judge learned of the holding, and
the court assumed he learned of it only after judgment. The court held that “it is reasonable to
question the partiality of a judge presiding over a case in which his spouse holds an ownership
interest in a party,” and it vacated the judgment. Id. Litovich is persuasive authority. Its reasoning

applies with greater force to a judge’s own reported holding.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 8 of 15 PagelD# 857

Central Telephone reached a different result on different facts. There, the shares came into
the judge’s portfolio through mergers of which he was unaware, were held in an IRA managed by
others, and were disclosed to the parties and sold promptly after the judge learned of them. 715
F.3d at 516-17. None of those facts appears here. The reports list the stock as a direct holding.
Judge Davis certified the holding in two consecutive annual reports, most recently in May 2026.
The docket reflects no disclosure to the parties.

Plaintiff does not contend that any ruling in this action evidences bias. Adverse rulings are
not the basis of this Motion. Section 455(a) “forbids more than actual bias.” DeTemple, 162 F.3d at
286. It asks what an informed outside observer would think of a judge deciding discovery directed
to a company whose stock the judge reported owning five months earlier. That observer would
question it.

C. Section 455(f) Does Not Eliminate the Need to Determine the Relevant Facts.

Section 455(f) relieves a judge of disqualification in defined circumstances. The matter
must have been assigned to the judge. The disqualifying interest must appear or be discovered
“after the matter was assigned to him or her.” Substantial judicial time must have been “devoted to
the matter.” The interest must be a financial interest in a party “other than an interest that could be
substantially affected by the outcome.” And the judge must “divest[] himself or herself of the
interest that provides the grounds for the disqualification.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(f); see Certain
Underwriter, 294 F.3d at 303. Each condition is a question of fact. The present record does not
resolve them.

Substantial judicial time. The Second Circuit measures substantial judicial time by
“examining the time and effort a district court invests in a matter,” not by counting calendar days.
Certain Underwriter, 294 F.3d at 304. The exception is unavailable “where the docket reflects little

time devoted to the matter.” Id. at 304-05 (describing Tramonte v. Chrysler Corp., 136 F.3d 1025,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 9 of 15 PagelD# 858

1031-32 (5th Cir. 1998)). The docket shows six orders by Judge Davis between September 9 and
October 7, 2026. Each is one or two pages. No hearing was held. ECF Nos. 63, 65. No report and
recommendation issued. Whether that participation is “substantial” within § 455(f) is for the Court
to determine on the record.

Appearance or discovery after assignment. Judge Davis signed the 2025 report on May 14
and May 26, 2026. This action was filed on July 30, 2026. The holding was reported before the
assignment existed. The record does not show when, if ever, Judge Davis identified the reported
holding as an interest in a party to this action. Plaintiff does not contend that § 455(f) is unavailable
merely because the stock was acquired or reported before assignment. Plaintiff contends that the
Court must state the timing before § 455(f) can be applied.

Nature of the interest. The reported value is $15,001 to $50,000. Plaintiff does not contend
that the outcome of this action could substantially affect the value of a holding in that range in a
company of Meta’s size. This condition does not by itself foreclose § 455(f).

Divestiture. The Federal Circuit, reviewing a judgment of this District, held that “to ‘divest’
oneself of ‘ownership’ of a legal or equitable interest is possible only if one is ‘deprived or
dispossesse[d]’ of ownership—something that is possible only if the interest is sold or given
away.” Centripetal, 38 F.4th 1025. Placing the stock in a blind trust did not qualify. Id. The court
vacated the rulings entered after the judge learned of the interest and directed reassignment,
observing that “[a]llowing the same judge to reaffirm his own rulings would severely undermine §
455, which is why cases are routinely reassigned upon vacatur of judgment under § 455.” Id. No
divestiture appears in this record. Plaintiff does not assume that one occurred. Plaintiff does not
assume that none occurred. The Motion asks the Court to state whether one occurred and when.

Mot. Part V(c).

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 10 of 15 PagelD#
859

Two further points follow. First, divestiture under § 455(f) does not by itself resolve the
effect of participation before it. “While Section 455(f) allows a judge to divest a newly-discovered
disqualifying interest and continue to preside over a case, that divestiture cannot cure
circumstances in which recusal was required years before and important decisions have been
rendered in the interim.” Litovich, 106 F.4th 218 (quoting Chase Manhattan Bank v. Affiliated FM
Ins. Co., 343 F.3d 120, 131 (2d Cir. 2003)). Whether curative divestiture is available once “a
litigation has advanced to substantive disputes” is “a determination that must be analyzed on a
case-by-case basis.” Id. Second, whether an order entered during a period of disqualification
should stand is a separate question from whether the judge may continue. The considerations for
that question are “the risk of injustice to the parties in the particular case, the risk that the denial of
relief will produce injustice in other cases, and the risk of undermining the public’s confidence in
the judicial process.” Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 864. That question is presented to the District Judge in
the companion application. It is not presented here.

D. The Motion Was Presented Promptly After Discovery.

“Timeliness is an essential element of a recusal motion.” United States v. Owens, 902 F.2d
1154, 1155 (4th Cir. 1990). A party “must raise the disqualification of the ... [judge] at the earliest
moment after knowledge of the facts.” Id. at 1156 (quoting Satterfield v. Edenton-Chowan Bd. of
Educ., 530 F.2d 567, 574-75 (4th Cir. 1975)). The rule exists “to prevent waste and delay” and to
prevent a party from awaiting an outcome before moving. Id. The Fourth Circuit applies that
requirement to motions under § 455(b) as well as § 455(a), and the judge’s independent obligation
does not excuse a party’s delay. Kolon Indus. Inc. v. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., 748 F.3d 160,
169-71 (4th Cir. 2014). Plaintiff was unaware of the reported interest when ECF No. 84 was
entered and at every earlier point in this action, and presented this Motion promptly after learning

of it, with no intervening ruling. Ballentine Decl. 2. That presentation satisfies Owens and Kolon.

10

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 87 Filed 10/13/26 Page 11 of 15 PagelD#
860

E. The Court Should Determine the Facts, Apply the Statute, and Transfer the
Referred Matters If Disqualification Is Required.

The Motion asks for five things. First, a statement on the record of the facts identified in
Part V of the Motion: the identity of the issuer, the dates of ownership, any divestiture, the manner
of holding, and any fact bearing on § 455(f). Second, a determination whether § 455(b)(4) or 8
455(a) requires disqualification on those facts. Third, priority determination, so that no further
substantive action is taken before the statutory question is resolved. Fourth, upon disqualification,
return or transfer of the referred matters through the Court’s assignment procedures. Fifth, a
written disposition sufficient to identify the grounds of decision.

The Motion does not ask Judge Davis to vacate any order. Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84 is
requested from District Judge Alston in the companion application, under the considerations
identified in Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at 864. The Motion does not ask Judge Davis to decide any
contested substantive matter after disqualification. The reassignment practice described in
Centripetal serves the same purpose here: the judge whose participation is questioned does not
revisit his own rulings.

IV. CONCLUSION

Two signed reports identify a holding of FB common stock. FB common stock is Meta
common stock. Meta is a party. Judge Davis has entered six orders in this action, one of which
decided discovery directed to Meta. Whether the holding continued into that period is the fact on
which § 455(b)(4) turns. Section 455(a) requires an objective assessment of the same
circumstances, whether or not knowledge is established. The Court should state the facts on the
record, apply § 455 to them, disqualify if the statute requires it, and transfer the referred matters

through the Court’s assignment procedures.
